From queer narratives to secret histories, this year celebrates the underground and the unheralded. Our writer uncovers so many stories, he feels like Columbo

By the time you’re done with Edinburgh art festival you’ll have uncovered so many hidden stories you’ll feel like Columbo. We’re talking queer narratives, secret histories, undiscovered archives: the whole festival is a celebration of the underground and unheralded. You can’t walk into a gallery without learning about some subcultural genius or longlost creative you’ve never heard of. That’s not a bad MO for a city-wide art festival.

But EAF is also a big, unwieldy, confusing thing. There are curated displays, satellite exhibitions, performances, off-site projects, and it’s impossible to figure out how any of it fits together. You’ve just got to follow your nose and hope you sniff out something you like. And you’d better like photography, because there’s a lot of it here.

items.title: Hillborg: Lost Landscapes album review – sonic imagination and luminous colours
items.blurb:
Gothenburg Symphony Orchestra/Kuusisto/Lubman/Falk Winland
(Alpha)
Unconventional instrumentation adds to the filmic feeling of these three works by the Swedish composer, played on this recording by a powerhouse orchestra on top form

Anders Hillborg’s stylistically eclectic work resists easy categorisation as these three rewarding works, performed by the Gothenburg Symphony Orchestra, demonstrate. Lost Landscapes opens with signature glissandi, features a filmic, jazz-inflected chase and ends in an orchestral death spiral. Pekka Kuusisto draws out its luminous colours and richly clustered harmonies.

The Strand Settings, a four-movement song cycle to texts by Canadian poet Mark Strand, was composed at the behest of Renée Fleming. Nature, the elements and a certain forlorn eroticism infuse poetry that Hillborg responds to with tonal and dynamic restraint. Gently pulsing strings with piquant woodwind and brass build atmospheric soundscapes over which Swedish soprano Ida Falk Winland spins haunting vocal lines in impeccable English.

items.title: Henry Threadgill, Vijay Iyer, Dafnis Prieto: Fifteen review – Pulitzer winner stirs gorgeous improv patterns
items.blurb:
(Nonesuch)
By turns gleeful, sensitive, urgent and ruminative, this is a brilliant set that plays to the trio’s formidable strengths

Though the century-old Pulitzer prize – launched as a celebration of the craft and social necessity of good news reportage – was eventually expanded to include fiction and music by 1943, the US-born art of jazz has only been represented by Ornette Coleman and Wynton Marsalis in their lifetimes, Duke Ellington, John Coltrane and Thelonious Monk posthumously – and most recently Henry Threadgill, for his four-part suite In for a Penny, In for a Pound, in 2016.

Publisher Joseph Pulitzer once declared his dreams for his readership were “to arrest their attention, enlist their sympathy … stimulate their imagination, convince their reason, and awaken their conscience”. Contemporary-classical composer and flautist Threadgill has been doing all that with his music, his personal story, his internationalism and his charisma since the 1960s. Now 82, he releases Fifteen, joining him in a brilliant trio featuring pianist/composer Vijay Iyer and creative Cuban percussionist Dafnis Prieto.

items.title: Open Mike Eagle and Kenny Segal: Doomed! review – caustic, crushing breakup album flirts with catharsis
items.blurb:
(Backwoodz)
The rapper-producer duo muster a breakup record with glistening beats and lovelorn lyrics that mull over grievances without resolve

Tough as they may be, breakups make for good material. Doomed! is Open Mike Eagle’s entry into that wide canon – sitting alongside Tyler, the Creator’s Igor and Ye’s 808s & Heartbreak in the alt-rap subcategory – and finds the LA-via-Chicago rapper every bit as wide-eyed, caustic and, at-times, crushing as those who’ve Kübler-Rossed their way out of a relationship before him. Out of lemons, lemonade, and all that.

In fact, without the disintegration of his five-year relationship, he and Kenny Segal – the feted Low End Theory-reared producer who helms the entire project – might have been resigned to merely cropping up as occasional features on each other’s records forever. The breakup gave sessions a focal point, and half a decade’s grievances to mull. Or, as Eagle puts it languidly over lounge glockenspiel on Streets of Rage: Public Arguments Edition: “These is true stories told loosely.”

items.title: Bruckner Symphony No 3 album review – Anima Eterna’s period instruments bring visceral drama
items.blurb:
Anima Eterna Brugge/Heras-Casado
(Harmonia Mundi)
There’s bone-crushing intensity in this striking recording of the original version of the Bruckner’s third. Pablo Heras-Casado teases out vital, almost operatic detail

According to legend, in the summer of 1873 Anton Bruckner travelled to Bayreuth intending to dedicate one of a pair of scores to his hero, Wagner. Apparently, the two composers got legless and by the time Bruckner arrived back home, he could no longer remember which symphony the master preferred. In a flap, he put pen to paper: “Symphony in D Minor, where the trumpet begins the theme?” he fished. “Yes! Best wishes! Richard Wagner,” was the reply.

With its mighty peaks and faint reminiscences of the operas, the Wagnerian aesthetic looms large over the Third Symphony in D minor, especially in its more radical original version, presented here by period instrument specialists Anima Eterna. Gut strings and original woodwind and brass are more pungent than their modern counterparts, but they sometimes struggle to summon the weight necessary for Bruckner. Not here. Pablo Heras-Casado conducts one of the most explosive and visceral accounts on record with his Belgian orchestra laying into the score with bone-crushing intensity.

items.title: LA Phil/Dudamel; Fantasia Orchestra / Fetherstonhaugh/Glennie reviews – high-contrast programming

Royal Albert Hall, London
The first of two evening proms began with the Los Angeles Philharmonic’s polished but polite Beethoven and intoxicating Adès. Later, the Fantasia orchestra’s bitty playlist-type programme only occasionally sparked into life.

This evening was, in a sense, a tale of two orchestras. On one hand, the international heavyweight, returning to the Proms for the first time in more than 20 years. On the other, the rapidly ascendant homegrown outfit founded while its members were still at school, already making its fourth Proms appearance.

Taking the early evening shift, the LA Phil and Gustavo Dudamel performed Beethoven’s Pastoral Symphony in an ultra-polished hybrid of period-performance style and modern instruments. String textures were a deluxe fine-knit, individual notes lifted but phrase endings subtly elongated so that the music seemed to breathe. The woodwind solos were cool and bright, offering further oxygenation to an already limpid sound, where massed trills spoke as one and countermelodies usually buried under orchestral busyness suddenly became audible.

items.title: ‘If we exhibited all the Balkan jokes, we wouldn’t have opened’: a trip to Slovenia’s Bullshit Museum
items.blurb:
In the heart of old Ljubljana, a mannequin with a bucket on its head welcomes visitors to a new and ambitious project – a museum focusing on the varied and sometimes antagonistic humour of the former Yugoslavia

On the main promenade along the river that runs through Ljubljana, Slovenia’s capital, tourists stop to photograph a mannequin with a bucket on its head. Dressed in a pistachio jacket and red leggings, the figure sits at a table in front of one of the houses in the historic Old Town, staring at a spilled cup of Turkish coffee, popular with Slovenes and with the other Balkan and central European citizens with whom they shared a country, until it collapsed in the early 1990s. A large sign in the background reads: “Bullshit Museum: The world is off the rails, and so are we. Yebiga!”

Yebiga, which can be loosely translated as “fuck it”, or “screw it”, is the red thread running through the museum that was launched in May and consists of five small rooms filled with mannequins wearing odd accessories, AI-generated images of laughing characters and scenes accompanying some of the jokes, framed or displayed on cardboard screens. The word encompasses the heart of Balkan humour, says the museum’s founder, Borut Kokelj, who wears a T-shirt emblazoned with the words: “What part of yebiga don’t you understand?”

items.title: Juilliard Orch/Royal Academy Symphony Orch / Salonen/Frang review – student players let rip, eventually
items.blurb:
Royal Albert Hall, London
Esa-Pekka Salonen led an orchestra of players from London’s Royal Academy of Music and New York’s Juilliard School through 20th-century classics with Vilde Frang the electrifying soloist in Berg’s Violin Concerto

Hot on the heels of the National Youth Orchestra’s Prom, here was another outstanding student ensemble: an orchestra recruited half-and-half from London’s Royal Academy of Music and New York’s Juilliard School, brought together by an exchange scheme funded by the RAM alumnus Elton John. Esa-Pekka Salonen took no prisoners as he whipped the players through three great 20th-century works.

They tore smartly into the start of Stravinsky’s Symphony in Three Movements, an exacting work requiring pinpoint-precise playing, which it mostly received. It felt as though Salonen was working hard to maintain that precision, though, and the performance didn’t quite achieve the buoyancy that would have let the music dance. Here and elsewhere in the programme, some of the music’s bright colours felt a little muted. Perhaps, for all Salonen’s guidance, this is one area in which there is no substitute for years of experience – in the ability to play to a venue and, for the wind and brass principals in particular, to fill a hall of this size not only with the instrument’s sound but with its character.

Playing their biggest headlining gig to date, the Russell brothers are in a bouncy mood, though their grandstanding rave melodies lose some punch in an outdoor environment

In the age of shortform video supremacy, there has been a great deal of angst about the authentic club music experience being rendered a vapid spectacle. Stop expecting DJs to be social media stars, put your phones away on the dancefloor, close your eyes and lose yourself in the beats, goes the revanchist wisdom.

It’s understandable, but worries about superstar DJs stomping on the face of the pure rave experience are almost 30 years old now. It is decades since the Prodigy, Chemicals, Orbital and Fatboy Slim lit up festival stages and the charts. And anyway, spectacles can be fun – and funny – and so can dance music.

items.title: The hill I will die on: Radio 4’s Today programme has become really annoying since I left | John Humphrys
items.blurb:
With its gushing interviewees and weird (y’know) ways of talking, the BBC news flagship show I used to present now has me harrumphing at the radio

It’s seven years since I stopped presenting the Today programme and started listening to Radio 3 instead. Or at least, that was the plan. On the first day it lasted for almost an hour. By the second day I’d given up on it. I suppose it was inevitable. You can’t spend 61 years as a news hack – more than half of it presenting the same programme – and then just erase it from your memory and start a new life.

What you can do in my own case – or, rather, can’t help doing – is mutate into a “new” listener. How to describe this “new” listener? I suppose if I were Today’s editor, the phrase “pain in the arse” might come to mind. Having been the one on the radio informing (and possibly sometimes annoying) the listeners for 33 years, I’m now the man shouting at his radio about how irritating the programme has become.

items.title: Humans have learned to fear ‘bugs’, but we shouldn’t – life as we know it hinges on invertebrates | Chris Packham
items.blurb:
At this point of the crisis in our relations with the natural world, we’ve got to protect these creatures – and we are running out of time

  • Read more from the Guardian’s invertebrate of the year 2026

Too many animals are regarded as “bugs”. And, if anything is a bug, it is a short step to it becoming a “pest”. Too many of us have a learned fear – it’s not innate – of anything with six legs or antennae.

I’m a big fan of the invertebrates and I love the Guardian’s invertebrate of the year competition because it focuses people’s attention on the little things rather than the typical animal superstars – the pandas, tigers and orangutans. In their diversity and varied ecology, the million-plus invertebrates on our planet often lead far more intricate and interesting lives than large animals with spines, like us. We urgently need to generate a much broader awareness of their beauty and importance. All these small creatures are as integral a part of our ecosystems as the fluffy things that we may want to put on our calendars.

items.title: Destructive and delicious: how an invasive deer in Hawaii is being turned into dinner
items.blurb:
The overpopulation of axis deer has taken an environmental toll, but Maui Nui Venison sees it as a resource instead of a pest

In 1868, the government of Hong Kong gave eight axis deer to Hawaii’s King Kamehameha V. They were a beautiful gift, these creatures that hail from south Asia, with their honey-colored pelts marked by a smattering of white spots. But their incursion into Maui started much later, in the 1950s, when they were brought to the island for recreational hunters.

Now, more than a century after their introduction, an estimated 60,000 traverse the Hawaiian islands of Lanai, Maui and Molokai in herds that are reshaping the environment. Unlike the white-tailed deer common along the US east coast, whose breeding season lasts from October to January, axis deer breed year-round. Their herds are constantly reduplicating. They feast on native grasses and endangered plants, chewing them down to their roots, leaving wide swathes of lands fallow. They can leap 10ft over fencing or barrel through it, consuming farmers’ crops and the cattle feed needed for Maui’s small beef industry.

items.title: Country diary: All hail the horsetail, a plant that could survive anything | Kate Blincoe
items.blurb:
Newton Flotman, Norfolk: It looks like a toilet brush yet predates the dinosaurs. I can’t help but give it a stroke by the roadside, even if I get strange looks

The rural road is flanked with a bank of green fuzz. It’s jungly and verdant – lush in a landscape that has turned brown and yellow from drought. I run my hand over the green bristles erupting from a bamboo-like stem.

Equisetum arvense, or field horsetail, looks fluffy, but it is wiry and rough. One could serve effectively as a toilet brush. The bristles are rich in abrasive silicon, which gives the texture of sandpaper. This explains another of equisetum’s common names, scouring rush, from when it was used to clean wood and polish metal. If you are careful, a hollow jointed stem can be separated at its junction and then rejoined like children’s tubular pipes for building, slotting back in a satisfying way.

items.title: The threatening thaw: climate professor on heatwave risks to tipping point of permafrost
items.blurb:
Prof Gustaf Hugelius warns wildfires could accelerate release of methane and carbon as vast regions approach irreversible thresholds

Heatwaves and wildfires are not just scorching forests, they are adding to the tipping point risks in the world’s vast permafrost regions, which contain three times more carbon than all the living vegetation on Earth.

This is a major concern for Gustaf Hugelius, a professor at the Bolin Centre of Climate Research at Stockholm University, Sweden, and a leading authority on the risks from thawing tundra and peatlands. In this Q&A, he explains why the world should pay attention.

As the Guardian’s Caribbean correspondent, I sometimes encounter stories that everyone is talking about in the region, but are not on the radar of the international media. Today, I’m taking over the Long Wave to bring you one of those stories. This summer, Guyanese ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett has made history as the first Caribbean candidate for the prestigious post of United Nations secretary general. items.title: ‘Starve the beast’? The $40tn cost of Republicans’ false promises to cut spending
items.blurb:
The enormous US debt under Trump will hobble the next Democratic administration – just as the GOP planned

You could pin the US’s staggering $40tn in government debt to Donald Trump’s Keystone Cops-style governance. Tariffs he sold as a new source of revenue were struck down by the supreme court, forcing the government to return tens of billions of dollars to importers. Elon Musk’s “department of government efficiency” (Doge), ostensibly created to stop wasteful government spending, decimated federal programs and likely killed millions of children, but did nothing to close the budget deficit. The burst of inflation following Trump’s misguided adventure in Iran sharply raised the cost of serving the government’s obligations.

Yet as the federal debt hits an all-time high, up from about $35tn when Trump took office less than two years ago, it is worth noting that the US’s gargantuan indebtedness is in fact the product of a longstanding Republican strategy that took shape well before Trump could even dream about gold-plating the White House. It was called “starve the beast”.

items.title: Relax, everyone: Elon Musk has a mantra to make the climate crisis go away | Emma Brockes
items.blurb:
It’s simple, says the SpaceX boss – according to something called the ‘Kardashev scale’, we just have to move energy production ‘off-planet’

Next time the weather gives the UK 61 days without rain and we wonder idly if this is the end, there is a term we may whistle up to soothe us. Like murmuring the rosary, or putting our fingers in our ears and humming, this phrase is to be mumbled on repeat – “the Kardashev scale, the Kardashev scale” – a buzzy concept in tech, much favoured by Elon Musk, and precisely the thing we’ve been waiting for. The Kardashev scale is the answer both to our impending doom and our anxiety around it – and if we decide to believe in it, we won’t have to give the climate crisis a single thought until the last drip falls from the tap.

This is the idea and it’s a familiar one to anyone who has watched tech billionaires take intractable, commonplace crises and decide that, among the measures and proposals in play, the vital missing ingredient so far has been them. Do you remember when Jeff Bezos, rather than doing something quotidian and loserish like funding public education by ensuring Amazon pays the same tax rate as regular Americans, decided instead to reinvent preschools?

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Football Daily | The Balogun affair and Premier League’s battle with conspiracy theorists
items.blurb:
Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

While Football Daily remains open to the idea that Stanley Kubrick directed the moon landings and the Pentagon is hiding grey aliens in Area 51, we have never had much truck with tinfoil hat-wearing conspiracy theorists when it comes to officiating in football. While refereeing a match in which all 22 participants are expert gaslighters will inevitably lead to mistakes, we’ve always presumed these gaffes can be attributed to good old-fashioned incompetence and not some shadowy cabal who have devoted their life’s work to keeping [insert your team’s name here] firmly in their place. Sadly, a random trawl of assorted Social Media Disgrace platforms on any given day during the season proves there is no shortage of paranoid fans, while “the Folarin Balogun affair” at the Geopolitics World Cup will have added no end of grist to their mill. After all, if an entitled president can successfully agitate to have a player’s suspension swept under the rug, who’s to say dark forces aren’t also at play when it comes to deciding whether the ball went out for a throw-in off Gabriel Martinelli or Enzo Le Fée?

May I be among 1,057 others born in the 1980s to mention that one of Orson Welles’ final film roles was as the voice of Unicron in Transformers: The Movie. His character was an enormous planet which travelled through space, devouring other planets. If that isn’t a suitable metaphor for the Premier League and its transfer windows, I don’t know what is” – Luke Davydaitis (and no others).

I wonder if West Ham and Wolves fans are regretting ever complaining that they had to wait for the last day of Big Website’s Premier League previews? And if Tottenham fans will take it as a hint that said complaining may lead to no preview at all” – Doug Peters.

If Carlos Baleba ends up at Manchester United, I hope we can rely on their fans to finally deliver the ‘Daydream Baleba’ chant the world deserves” – Chris Jersan.

items.title: Michele Tafoya: from unassuming NFL sideline reporter to rightwing firebrand
items.blurb:
The former Sunday Night Football stalwart is now one step from a seat in the US Senate. And she could cause a shock in liberal Minnesota

As the third leg of NBC’s Sunday Night Football crew alongside play-by-play man Al Michaels and the tart-tongued analyst Cris Collinsworth, Michele Tafoya was a paragon of deference and neutrality for 11 years as an NFL sideline reporter, dutifully relating boilerplate tactics, talking points and injury updates when she wasn’t nodding along to softball interviews or fumbling through hammy production gimmicks for viewers who might have been too offline to get the bit. She was almost pathologically committed to not doing anything to draw attention to herself or her gender in an era when sideline reporting was a fast track to national celebrity. Even her football takes hewed to the middle. (“New Orleans doesn’t want to lose to Atlanta twice in a season …”) Anyone who says they saw the 61-year-old emerging as a rightwing firebrand was watching a different game.

And yet here we are. Last week, Tafoya was the decisive winner of Minnesota’s US Senate Republican primary, earning the party’s nomination for November’s general election. Even more striking: she beat back eight challengers, not least Adam Schwarze, the party-endorsed pro-gun, pro-military ex-Navy SEAL, and Royce White, the anti-leftist, anti-trans NBA flameout currently testing WNBA gender norms.

Spaniard loses narrowly in fourth round of the Cincinnati Open yet the buzz around him will only get louder

As Rafael Jódar slowly trudged from the court, he could only bring himself to wave at his adoring crowd for no more than a millisecond. The 19-year-old was appropriately devastated after he had come within two points of victory on numerous occasions before losing 4-6, 7-6 (3), 6-3 in the fourth round of the Cincinnati Open to an excellent Flavio Cobolli.

No matter, Jódar departs Ohio having further solidified himself as the subject of so much conversation on the ATP Tour. This has been a turbulent and unpredictable year in men’s tennis, largely thanks to Carlos Alcaraz’s extended injury layoff. The one certainty through it all has been the imperious rise of Jódar. After a short period competing at the University of Virginia, Jódar started to play regularly on the tour only in May last year. In August 2025, he was ranked No 540. He began the 2026 season at No 165.

One win in England’s last 17 Tests. Those were the numbers that greeted Brendon McCullum and Ben Stokes when they took over in 2022, a reminder of just how bad things had ended under Joe Root. It was a statistic that gave the new boys permission to rip up the old order.

So it’s easy to forget that precious one. It was near the middle of that horror run, and it came at Headingley against India five years ago this month. The tourists were bowled out for 78 as Root reached three figures and celebrated his 27th victory as Test captain, a record among Englishmen. The Yorkshireman had to come home to find some breathing space.

items.title: The Spin | Heatwaves leave groundstaff high and dry in search of playable wickets
items.blurb:
A summer of five heatwaves and barely a drop of rain have left groundstaff wrung out as they work all hours to keep packed schedule going

On Thursday, the County Championship resumes for its final six-week run, charging towards 27 September with barely a pause for breath. It’s tight at the top of Division One, with only 11 points between first placed Nottinghamshire and sixth placed Essex, while Kent and Northants prepare to elbow it out for the second Division Two promotion place alongside almost-inked-in Durham.

The players, on the treadmill since 3 April, and switching between competitions, are run ragged. But no one is as wrung out as the groundstaff, dealing with a summer of fiery extremes, five heatwaves, excruciating temperatures and barely a drop of rain across most of England. In the words of the Met Office scientist Mike Kendon, “the climate of the 20th century has now gone” but the cricket season is expecting to roll on by as if nothing is happening. The Spin asked three head groundsmen how they are coping.

The 2,000 Guineas winner exited the racing stage as the world’s top-rated three-year-old on a mark of 127, just 4lb behind the joint top-rated older horses, Ka Ying Rising and Ombudsman, and with the scope and untapped potential to match or exceed them before the end of the campaign.

A void, though, can also be a vacancy and Constitution River, the second-best three-year-old so far this year, will have an immediate opportunity to step into the breach when he lines up against Ombudsman, in what promises to be a memorable renewal of the International Stakes on the opening afternoon of York’s Ebor festival on Wednesday.

Long before Amy Hunt catapulted herself into the mainstream by winning an unprecedented four gold medals at the European Championships, she was remarkably upfront about her ambitions. There was no coyness. No equivocation. She wanted the quadruple in Birmingham. And having talked a good game, she delivered.

She celebrated her final golden night in Birmingham with a glass of champagne and a KFC, as well as a 2am massage to ensure her legs would be fresh for her next race in Lausanne on Friday. It meant going to bed at 4am. But despite being on four hours sleep on Monday morning, she is sharp as a tack and explains why being bold is good for her – and her sport.

As England’s batting coach for a good deal of Joe Root’s first spell as Test captain, I saw directly how conscientious he was in the role. It was impossible not to feel for him at the end, when results dried up and he was almost alone on a burning deck.

Whenever I am asked who my favourite current cricketer is, I struggle to look beyond Root. He is such a grounded individual and clearly a fabulous player. He is also his own best coach, always first in the nets and last out of them, forever thinking about his game and how to improve those one-percenters.

items.title: Wicket: Beyond the boundary – a photo essay
items.blurb:
Through the Royal Photographic Society’s Eamonn McCabe bursary programme, Nathan McGill set out to explore women’s cricket across Bradford. What emerged was a close and extended engagement with one club: Bradford Park Avenue Ladies Cricket Club

Interest in women’s cricket is expanding rapidly across the country. Attendance and viewing figures for this year’s Women’s T20 World Cup in England reached an all-time high, while the recent Test at Lord’s set an attendance record for a women’s Test match. This month, the Hundred match between London Spirit and Southern Brave set a new record for a women’s group game. Yet visual culture often struggles to keep pace. Historic archives remain sparse, although growing interest is creating a richer contemporary record – one to which this project, Wicket, contributes.

Wicket is rooted in relationships and place. The project puts women and girls at the centre of the narrative, creating images that foreground not only participation but belonging, camaraderie and community. Bradford Park Avenue Ladies is a visibly diverse, intergenerational team shaped by a range of lived experiences – a reflection of Bradford’s social fabric, though still largely absent from mainstream images of cricket.

Every summer a group set up camp at Colwall, the real home of women’s cricket, and spend five days playing the sport they love

Many places have claimed to be the home of women’s cricket over the years. Taunton did so in 2006 when the England and Wales Cricket Board named it as the new “permanent” base of the England Women’s team – a deal that proved anything but permanent. Lord’s recently attempted to claim the moniker, after hosting one women’s Test in 142 years.

The real home of women’s cricket, however, is a small village in Herefordshire, on the western side of the Malvern Hills: Colwall.

items.title: In a Himalayan Village, This Couple Replaced School for Nature, Travel & Carpentry to Raise Their 3 Kids
items.blurb: This story is part of “ Parenting: What Google Won’t Tell You” — The Better India’s people-led parenting series that goes beyond conventional advice to document how real families are actually raising their children. Through real parents, parenting coaches, influencers and experts, the series brings honest, diverse and relatable perspectives on the questions, choices, challenges and solutions that shape everyday parenting — the things Google can’t always answer. The aroma of simmering broth drifts through the mountain air as laughter rises from a rooftop kitchen in a small Himachal village. Around the table, travellers from different parts of the world chop vegetables and trade stories while three children move easily among them, helping with dinner, listening, asking questions and joining the conversation. For Mayur and Joy Sontakke, moments like these are part of how their children learn. The Indian-Vietnamese couple have built much of their family life around NomadGao, the coliving and coworking community they created for digital nomads. Here, their 13-year-old twin boys and eight-year-old daughter learn through shared meals, conversations with travellers, baking experiments, board games, carpentry projects and long afternoons outdoors. The couple, who also run The Hotpot House in Dharamkot, chose during the pandemic to step away from conventional schooling and adopt a more flexible, child-led approach to education. Their idea of learning now stretches across kitchens, farms, workshops, books, conversations and everyday life, shaped by curiosity rather than a fixed curriculum. Building a life around community Long before NomadGao existed, Mayur was questioning conventional ideas about education and success. Growing up in Kolhapur in a traditional middle-class family, he followed the expected path until he found himself increasingly disconnected from what he was being taught. “I was disillusioned about why I was learning what I was learning,” he recalls. Failing Class 12, which many considered a life-defining setback, became a turning point instead. “That was the best thing,” he says. “Everyone lost their expectations from me. I felt free to do whatever I wanted.” At NomadGao in Himachal, Mayur and Joy’s three children have grown up surrounded by travellers, conversations and new experiences. The years that followed were filled with unconventional experiences: door-to-door marketing in villages, part-time jobs, remote work, and eventually travelling across India and Southeast Asia as one of the country’s early digital nomads. Those experiences reinforced a belief that some of life’s most important lessons happen outside classrooms. Joy’s journey was equally transformative. Raised in Vietnam, she followed a conventional route through school, university, and a banking career before meeting Mayur in 2017. After moving to India, she found herself exploring entirely new paths — from nutrition and health coaching to toy design and eventually running a restaurant. “I’m a self-learner,” she says. “Everything I learned in school or university didn’t always matter in what I chose to do later.” Together, they built NomadGao as a space where remote workers could live, work, and connect with like-minded people. What began as a dream quickly grew into a thriving community in Goa and later Himachal Pradesh. Their children grew up alongside it. Rethinking what education could look like While the pandemic pushed many families to reconsider education, Mayur and Joy had already been having those conversations. For Mayur, the shift stemmed from a growing belief that traditional education was struggling to keep pace with a rapidly changing world. “I learned a lot more travelling and meeting people than I did sitting in a classroom,” he says. The family’s circumstances also played a role. The twin boys, who had moved from Vietnam to India, did not initially speak English. Sending them straight into a conventional school environment felt overwhelming. At the same time, the family wanted the flexibility to spend time in both India and Vietnam, participating fully in festivals, traditions, and family life. Joy was the one who first introduced the idea of unschooling. She had come across the concept while reflecting on her experiences as a parent. Watching her youngest daughter thrive through a baby-led approach to eating made her rethink how children learn best. The twins began cooking with Mayur when they were young. Today, preparing meals is one of the ways the children build independence and essential life skills. “I saw the difference between forcing active learning and allowing children to learn naturally,” she says. “For me, unschooling is not about avoiding school. It’s about learning how to learn by yourself.” That idea became the foundation of their parenting philosophy. Instead of focusing on what children should learn at a particular age, they focus on helping them discover how they learn best. What does a school day look like without school? Ask Mayur what a typical school day looks like in their home and he laughs. “There isn’t really one.” Learning changes depending on where the family is and what is happening around them. In Vietnam, that might mean spending time on farms. When the family was building their home, learning involved carpentry and hands-on construction work. Today, in Himachal Pradesh, their children’s days include a blend of structured learning and self-directed exploration. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Nomadtuktuk -Travel - Unschool (@nomadtuktuk) Mornings are often dedicated to maths and English. Afternoons are spent outdoors, reading, drawing, sketching, cooking, baking, or playing with local children. The family does not follow a rigid curriculum, but they do provide resources and guidance when interests emerge. When the boys developed a passion for baking, their parents found ways to nurture it. When drawing captured their attention, online art courses entered the picture. At NomadGao, meals often bring the children together with travellers from different countries, turning dinner into an opportunity to exchange stories, cultures and ideas. “As long as I give them resources, they’ll figure it out,” says Mayur. Not every experiment succeeds. The twins struggled with traditional approaches to English and maths. Textbooks failed to spark interest. So the family adapted. Today, journaling, storytelling, tutors, and interest-led projects play a larger role. For Joy, flexibility is key. “Success is not about how much you learn,” she says. “It’s about the journey that you enjoy.” The world becomes the classroom One of the most distinctive aspects of the family’s approach is the environment they have created around their children. At NomadGao, guests from around the world arrive with vastly different life stories and experiences. Some stay for weeks. Others remain for months. Many become part of the family’s daily life. Instead of spending all day with peers their own age, the children regularly interact with entrepreneurs, artists, engineers, travellers, and remote workers from different countries. An Israeli automation engineer who stayed at NomadGao spent time with the children, introducing them to technology, another culture and a different way of looking at the world. “When kids go to school, they mostly interact with people of the same age,” says Mayur. “But when they spend time with people from different generations, the learning becomes explosive .” He recalls an Israeli automation engineer who stayed at NomadGao for several months and spent significant time with the children. Through those conversations, they learned about technology, another culture, another country, and another way of life. Another regular guest introduced them to board games and strategic thinking. Others have shared stories of travel, work, creativity, and personal challenges. Many visitors are surprised by how easily the children engage with adults. Lessons from the kitchen The family’s restaurant, The Hotpot House, has become another unexpected learning space. Although neither parent initially imagined opening a restaurant, it has evolved into a place where the children observe real-world problem-solving, communication, and responsibility in action. Hospitality, Mayur believes, teaches lessons that are difficult to replicate elsewhere. “It teaches compassion and patience at the same time,” he says. “Some guests are difficult, but you still have to serve them with kindness .” The children occasionally help around the restaurant, observe daily operations, and witness the realities of running a business. More importantly, they see their parents model teamwork, resilience, and service. Moving between India and Vietnam has given the children opportunities to learn through farms, festivals, family traditions and the different cultures they encounter along the way. Cooking has become a particularly important life skill. The boys started cooking with Mayur at a young age, often experimenting together in the kitchen. Today, dinner preparation frequently falls to the children themselves. For the couple, these experiences matter just as much as academic learning. “I don’t want my kids to grow up without life skills,” Mayur says. “Cooking, cleaning, taking responsibility – all of these are equally important.” ‘Parents should think about their own inner child’ The decision to unschool has brought its share of challenges. Extended family members continue to question their choices. Friends occasionally express concern. There are practical difficulties too, particularly when it comes to finding a community of children following similar educational paths. Living in a village means most local children attend conventional schools and have limited free time. “There’s still a challenge around social life,” admits Mayur. Despite those hurdles, the family remains committed to the path they have chosen. In their children, they see qualities they deeply value: curiosity, independence, confidence around adults, a love of reading, and a willingness to explore new interests without fear of failure. As the future of work and learning continues to evolve, they believe one skill matters above all else. “Learning is democratised now,” says Mayur. “If you want to learn something, the resources are there. The important thing is learning how to learn.” For parents curious about alternative education but hesitant to take the first step, their advice is simple. For Mayur and Joy, unschooling is not about removing education from their children’s lives. It is about giving them the confidence to follow their curiosity and figure out how they learn best. “There is risk in every path,” Mayur says. “Traditional schooling has risks too. You have to choose your own bets.” Joy offers a gentler reflection. “I want parents to think about their own inner child,” she says. “What did you want when you were young? Then try to create that kind of environment for your children.” Back in the kitchen, dinner is finally ready. Conversations continue long after the meal is served. Stories are shared, questions are asked, and new ideas emerge. Perhaps that is what Mayur and Joy are trying to give their children: the confidence to meet the world with curiosity, and the ability to keep learning from it. All images courtesy Mayur Sontakke

items.title: Sacred Forests, Ancient Rules: How India’s Communities Have Protected Nature for Centuries
items.blurb: In many parts of India, entering a forest once meant entering the home of a deity. It also meant stepping onto land where a tree could not be cut, an animal could not be hunted and, in some places, even fallen wood could not be taken away. The rules were rarely written down. Instead, they travelled through stories, rituals, festivals and warnings passed from one generation to the next. Today, scientists have another vocabulary for these places: biodiversity refuges, carbon stores, water catchments and ecological corridors. India has another, older vocabulary. Devarakadu in Karnataka. Kavu in Kerala. Oran in Rajasthan. Sarna or Jaherthan in Jharkhand. Law Kyntang in Meghalaya. Umang Lai in Manipur. Dev Van in Himachal Pradesh. Different landscapes and different communities, but a shared idea: some forests are not ours to use freely. As forests are increasingly fragmented for roads, infrastructure and other forms of development, that old idea is finding new relevance. A forest with a boundary you cannot always see Sacred groves are patches of natural vegetation protected by communities because of their religious, cultural or spiritual significance. They can range from a handful of trees to village forests spread across several hectares. The rules vary from place to place. In some groves, cutting trees and hunting are completely prohibited. Elsewhere, communities may collect honey, medicinal plants or deadwood under customary rules. Because they are often less disturbed than surrounding landscapes, these groves can preserve native plants and animals that have disappeared elsewhere. Their tree cover can also help reduce soil erosion, retain moisture and support groundwater recharge. In dry landscapes, sacred commons can provide communities with grazing land, fodder and water. In other words, a centuries-old cultural practice can also protect an ecosystem — and that ecosystem, in turn, continues to support the community. The scale of this tradition, however, is difficult to pin down. The rules vary from place to place. In some groves, cutting trees and hunting are completely prohibited. Elsewhere, communities may collect honey, medicinal plants or deadwood under customary rules. Photograph: (The Wire Science) The CPR Environmental Education Centre has documented thousands of sacred groves across India. Its records list 13,270 groves, while older estimates suggest the actual number could be much higher. CPREEC itself notes that its documentation is not necessarily a final count and continues to work on their conservation and restoration. That uncertainty matters. Sacred groves are not always neatly marked parcels on a government map. Many are community-protected landscapes whose boundaries and rules exist primarily through customary knowledge. One idea, many names Travel from the Western Ghats to the Thar, and the name changes with the landscape. The idea, however, remains remarkably similar. In Karnataka, it is Devarakadu In Karnataka’s Malnad region, Devara Kadu are treated as more than forests. Traditionally, felling, lopping and clearing trees — and even removing weeds — are forbidden. The five natural elements are revered as part of nature worship. Yet these groves have been shrinking. A survey found that their area had fallen from around 15,000 acres to less than 9,000 acres by 2018. A New Indian Express report attributed the encroachments to factors including migration and the pursuit of economic returns. In Kerala, they are called Kavus Particularly common in Kannur and Kasaragod, Kerala’s Kavus have retained much of their original forest character and harbour native species. The Kerala State Biodiversity Board has now launched a pilot restoration programme covering five Kavus. More than 100 native and threatened plant species have been identified, with nearly 3,000 saplings planned for planting. Law Kyntang and Umang Lai in the Northeast In Meghalaya, the Khasi community protects sacred groves known as Law Kyntang or Law Lyngdoh through customary traditions. Researchers from Assam Royal Global University found that the Law Kyntang Ryngkew Swer Sacred Grove stores more than 100 megagrams of carbon per hectare, with the densest patches reaching up to 200 Mg/ha. In Manipur, sacred forests associated with deities are known as Umang Lai. Around 365 groves have been reported across the state, although recent research points to growing pressure from urban expansion. In Jharkhand, Sarna or Jaherthan In Jharkhand, sacred forest patches are known as Sarna or Jaherthan and are central to tribal worship. Last year, hundreds of Adivasis in traditional attire formed a human chain in Ranchi, waving the red-and-white flags of the Sarna faith and protesting the recently completed ramp of the Siram Toli-Meccon flyover. The CPR Environmental Education Centre has documented thousands of sacred groves across India. Photograph: (Ecoldealz) Their concern was that the ramp ended just feet from a Kendriya Sarna Sthal , a central sacred grove that draws lakhs of visitors each year. Sal ( Shorea robusta ) is sacred in many such groves, although other species also occur. In East Singhbhum, Santhal and Bhumij communities call these sacred spaces Jaherthan , where Sal and mahua ( Madhuca longifolia ) are among the trees found. The Thar has Orans Nowhere is the ecological value of sacred landscapes more striking than Rajasthan. The Orans of the Thar may look very different from the dense forests of Kerala or Meghalaya. Yet they perform many of the same functions. The Supreme Court’s December 2024 judgment noted that Rajasthan has around 25,000 Orans covering approximately six lakh hectares, with about 5.37 lakh hectares located in the western Thar. These landscapes provide grazing areas, forest produce, medicinal plants and water. They also help protect springs, ponds and groundwater systems. Today, they face a new question: how can land needed for India’s clean-energy transition coexist with community-protected ecosystems? The question has become particularly visible around solar and wind projects in western Rajasthan, where pastoral communities depend on grasslands and commons. Conservationist and camel herder Sumer Singh Bhati, whom The Better India recently spoke to, has highlighted community concerns that large-scale solar development could damage grasslands and native grasses such as sewan and dhaman, on which livestock depend. The issue, therefore, is not simply development versus conservation. It is also about recognising what already exists on the land — including its ecological functions and community rights. A court draws the line That is where the Supreme Court’s 18 December 2024 judgment becomes significant. While hearing a case concerning Rajasthan’s sacred groves, the Court directed the state to conduct on-ground and satellite mapping of sacred groves, including Orans, Dev-vans and Rundhs, and complete their survey and notification across districts. Crucially, it said their classification should not depend on their size. Their cultural and ecological significance should matter. The Court also directed that the groves be classified as forests in accordance with the Central Empowered Committee’s recommendations and suggested protection under the Wildlife Protection Act’s community-reserve framework . In dry landscapes, sacred commons can provide communities with grazing land, fodder and water. Photograph: (Félix Landry Yuan.) It was an important recognition of something communities had understood for generations: A forest does not become valuable only when it is large enough to appear on a map. For centuries, these communities have protected patches of nature not through formal conservation plans, but through belief, custom and collective responsibility. The names may change from one region to another. So do the rituals and rules. But the underlying principle remains the same: some parts of nature are worth protecting simply because they sustain life — and because they are not ours to destroy. Sources: ‘Sacred Groves, the secret wizards of conservation’ : By Aarushi Wadhwa, Published on 28 August 2023 ‘Why Reserve Forests Must Be Saved from Religious Encroachment for Peaceful Coexistence’ : By Naorem Mohen, Published on 2 December 2025 ‘Karnataka: God’s own forests watch over Kodagu’ : By Prajna G R, Published on 17 June 2018 ‘Programme in place to restore sacred groves in Kerala’ : By Sarath Babu George, Published on 30 April 2026

items.title: After a Decade Cleaning the Himalayas, He’s Sending 1 Kg of Waste Back With Each Kedarnath Pilgrim
items.blurb: Every year, millions of people make the steep climb to Kedarnath. This year, environmental activist Pradeep Sangwan wants them to carry something back with their memories: a kilogram of waste. The founder of Healing Himalayas, a non-profit that has spent years cleaning trekking routes across the Indian Himalayas, believes a simple shift in behaviour could transform one of India's busiest pilgrimage corridors. Through a campaign called #CarryMeBack, Sangwan is asking every pilgrim travelling to Kedarnath to pick up and bring back at least a kilogram of waste on their return journey. The maths behind the idea If one lakh pilgrims carry back one kilogram each, that is 100 tonnes of waste removed from the mountains. Sangwan shared the vision on social media. "Forty days of Kedarnath Yatra. Ten lakh registered pilgrims reached, breaking all previous records. Our Carry Me Back Yatra is now picking up. One lakh yatri carrying one kg equals 100 tons removed. That's our aim." View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) The campaign is digitally tracked, allowing volunteers to record participation and measure impact in real-time. In a region where waste management remains one of the biggest challenges of mass tourism , the idea has struck a chord. When pilgrimage leaves a trail behind As visitor numbers rise every year, so does the volume of discarded plastic bottles, food packaging, raincoats, glass containers and other waste generated along the route. In previous years, photographs from the pilgrimage corridor have shown piles of garbage accumulating near campsites and resting points, highlighting the strain placed on an ecologically sensitive landscape. For Sangwan, the problem is one he has witnessed first-hand for more than a decade. "On my visits to the region, I was both irked and saddened to see the piles of garbage disfiguring famous trekking spots," he told Outlook Traveller in an earlier interview. If one lakh pilgrims carry back one kilogram each, that is 100 tonnes of waste removed from the mountains. Photograph: (Instagram/@pradeep_sangwan_ (Enhanced using AI)) Rather than wait for a solution, he began carrying waste back himself. Friends and family joined him on clean-up treks. What started as a personal effort gradually grew into a movement. In 2016, he founded the Healing Himalayas Foundation , which today conducts clean-up drives, waste audits, awareness campaigns and waste-management initiatives across mountain regions. But even after years of collecting trash, Sangwan realised that clean-ups alone could not solve the problem. The solution to this problem, he believes, lies in participation. Turning pilgrims into partners The campaign turns every traveller into part of the solution. Sangwan has repeatedly emphasised that participants do not need to carry large quantities of waste. Even a few hundred grams can make a difference when multiplied across lakhs of visitors. "Yes — 250 grams to 5 kg should be carried back by yatris and pilgrims. That's the campaign," he explained online. The idea turns passive concern into practical action. At Kedarnath alone, the organisation recently reported handling 25 tonnes of segregated and baled material through its material recovery facility. Photograph: (Instagram/@pradeep_sangwan_ (Enhanced using AI)) A plastic bottle picked up during a trek may seem insignificant. But when thousands of people do the same thing, the cumulative impact becomes substantial. Within just ten days of the campaign gaining momentum, hundreds of travellers reportedly helped remove more than 1,000 kilograms of waste from the Kedarnath route. The early results offered a glimpse of what collective action could achieve during a pilgrimage season that sees enormous footfall. Clean-ups are a ‘postmortem’ For Sangwan, however, carrying waste back is only one part of a larger conversation. Recently, he highlighted the presence of nearly a tonne of discarded glass bottles at Kedarnath and questioned how such material was reaching high-altitude regions in the first place. "Carry it back if at all it is being consumed," he urged, adding that his team was auditing brands to better understand waste streams in the area. He has also repeatedly called for greater attention to waste minimisation at source, segregation systems, infrastructure and scientific disposal. Within just ten days of the campaign gaining momentum, hundreds of travellers reportedly helped remove more than 1,000 kilograms of waste from the Kedarnath route. Photograph: (Instagram/@pradeep_sangwan_ (Enhanced using AI) "What we do is postmortem by collecting it," he noted. "But the question is how do we control it at the foothills?" According to Sangwan, effective waste management in the mountains rests on four pillars: minimisation, source segregation and infrastructure, public participation, and reverse supply chains that ensure waste is transported and processed responsibly. The Carry Me Back campaign fits into that larger framework by addressing the participation gap. What thousands of return journeys can do Healing Himalayas’ waste audits reveal the scale of material already being recovered and processed. At Kedarnath alone, the organisation recently reported handling 25 tonnes of segregated and baled material through its material recovery facility. The waste included multilayer plastic, PET bottles, cardboard, cloth, raffia bags, HDPE, paper plates, raincoats and other discarded items. What is #CarryMeBack ? Lakhs of pilgrims visit Kedarnath every year. If even 10,000 people carry back 2.5 kg each, that’s 25,000 kg of waste returning to the right place Let’s support the campaign Share this with anyone visiting Kedarnath. #CarryMeBack . pic.twitter.com/NL7pbzaBe7 — Pradeep Sangwan (@iPradeepSangwan) June 7, 2026 More than 5.5 tonnes of that material, Sangwan noted, came through the Carry Me Back initiative itself. Yet the campaign's significance extends beyond the numbers. It reframes a pilgrimage as an act of stewardship. A kilogram may not sound like much. But in the hands of a lakh pilgrims, it becomes 100 tonnes. About the campaign This story is part of The Better India’s #CivicSenseHeroes , a year-long nationwide campaign celebrating citizens who take responsibility for the places and communities we all share. From cleaner streets and safer roads to restored lakes and public spaces, we’re looking for everyday Indians turning civic sense into action. Know someone doing work like this? Nominate your Civic Sense Hero here .

items.title: What Every Tourist Should Know Before Visiting India's High-Risk Travel Spots
items.blurb: You're driving up toward a high pass in Ladakh, and the road ahead is blocked. No warning sign, no clear explanation at first glance — just a stretch of tarmac that's been cordoned off, and a small queue of vehicles waiting to find out why. It's the kind of moment that plays out on high-altitude roads across Ladakh, Kashmir and India's border states every single day. A stretch closes, a soldier or road official explains why, and the traveller is left to either wait it out or take a detour. That scene is also, roughly, what's playing out in a video doing the rounds again this month — a traveller in Ladakh questioning why the road ahead was blocked. Strip away the noise around it, and it's a useful reminder of something worth knowing before you book: for a certain kind of Indian holiday, this is simply part of the itinerary. That's the part most people don't plan for until they're standing at the barrier — not just the permits and IDs, but the very real chance that the road itself won't cooperate. Here's why both of these show up so often in these regions, and how to plan around them well before you leave home. Ladakh and Kashmir: what the checkpost actually wants from you Ladakh and Kashmir sit close enough to international borders that the government keeps a close watch on who travels through them. Until 2021, every I ndian citizen entering inner Ladakh needed an Inner Line Permit, checked at army posts along some of the highest roads in the country. That permit has since been replaced by an Environment and Development Fee, which is worth applying for online well in advance and carrying as a printed receipt, since a payment confirmation on its own isn't always accepted. The checkpost process itself hasn't really changed: at South Pullu and Khaltsar, you'll still need to show that receipt alongside a valid government photo ID before you're waved through — so it helps to keep that ID on you at all times, not just for hotel check-in. The safest way to explore high-risk mountain routes is to plan for uncertainty, from carrying printed documents to checking weather conditions before each leg of the journey. Photograph: (Facebook) Foreign nationals and Overseas Citizens of India need a Protected Area Permit instead, best started early through a registered local agent. Seasoned solotraveller Shruthika Parupalli, speaking about her first trip to Srinagar, described how unsettling the army presence felt at first — soldiers stationed every few hundred metres, ID checks at multiple points along the route. “By the end of the trip, it was this same visible security that had made me feel safest. It's a useful reminder that a heavy security presence in these regions is a planning detail, not a red flag. People should expect ID checks at several points on a single day's drive, build a few extra minutes into every leg of the journey for it, and it becomes routine within a day,” she says. The Northeast: same idea, different paperwork The Northeast works on a similar principle , just with different names on the form. Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland and Mizoram all require an Inner Line Permit for Indian citizens and a Protected Area Permit for foreign visitors, checked at the state border — best applied for online well ahead of arrival rather than at the checkpost itself. Assam doesn't require a domestic permit at all, which is why it tends to function as the gateway into this region, but foreign nationals still need to register with the local FRRO within 24 hours of arrival, and border-adjacent pockets of the state carry their own protected-area rules. If your trip strings together more than one Northeastern state, map the route first and budget time for a separate permit at each border — one folder rarely covers all of them. Even with the right papers, the weather gets the final say Getting your documents in order is only half the job. The other half is timing your trip around the season. Uttarakhand's Joshimath–Badrinath highway — the only road to Badrinath and the ancient village of Mana beyond it — runs along a slope that has never fully settled. Landslides shut it down almost every July and August, sometimes for days, while road crews work to clear the debris, which makes this exactly the window to build buffer days into a Char Dham itinerary rather than book it back to back. For travellers heading into the Northeast, permits can vary by state, making it important to map the route and paperwork before setting out. Photograph: ( Tirtha Yatra ) Journalist Sriroopa Dutta recalls being stopped by the Army on the road to Badrinath, about three to four kilometres short of Mana Gaon, India's last village on the Indo-Tibetan border, while travelling with her mother as a child. Their first assumption was that it had something to do with travelling as a woman — but the personnel was quick to clarify that it had nothing to do with a woman travelling without a male companion. The reason, as Dutta puts it, was simpler and more immediate: the terrain itself. Landslides and mudslides had made parts of the road unstable, and the Army was redirecting travellers rather than risk letting them cross the affected stretch. It's a small detail that captures the whole logic of these closures — as Dutta says, "a road that appears safe one moment can become dangerous after heavy rain, a landslide or a sudden mudslide," which is exactly why the Army has to make quick, on-the-ground calls, sometimes stopping people or rerouting traffic before conditions get worse. Rishi Juggi, a Bengaluru-based software engineer, saw the same pattern play out one state over, on a trip to Thachi valley in Himachal Pradesh, after locals had already warned her group that heavy rain could cut them off. It did. “Driving back toward Aut, our jeep slid across roads that had turned into streams overnight, and a stretch of hillside gave way just 15 to 20 metres behind us. That taught us to check the India Meteorological Department's forecast each morning instead of the night before, because a warning that arrives too late doesn't help at all. So I always urge travellers to stay on top of weather updates,” she says. Monsoon journeys through the Himalayas and Western Ghats require room for delays, as landslides can close key roads for hours or even days. Photograph: ( Tripoto ) This isn't only a Himalayan problem. The Western Ghats see it too — in July 2022, the Agumbe Ghat connecting Shivamogga and Udupi districts in Karnataka stayed shut to traffic for nearly two weeks after landslides hit two of its sharpest curves, sending vehicles on a long detour through Someshwara instead. It's the same lesson from a different range: book accommodation with flexible cancellation on any monsoon-season Ghats trip , because a single closed ghat road can turn a one-night stop into two with no warning at all, and look for travel insurance that specifically names landslide-related delays, since many standard policies leave that out. Before you hit "book" None of this should put you off travelling to these places — it should just change when you start planning. If you're headed to Ladakh, Kashmir or the Northeast, apply for your permits well ahead of time and carry printed copies with you, plus a spare tucked away separately, in case your main bag gets checked and set aside. A screenshot on a phone with low battery and no signal won't get you very far at a checkpost with patchy network. If you're driving through the Western Ghats or the Char Dham route in July or August, that same instinct applies to the weather: check forecasts daily, build in slack, and book stays you can shift without a penalty. A little preparation goes a long way here. The checkpost will be there next season too, and the slope above Joshimath will keep watching the sky the way it always has. The traveller who plans around both is the one who actually gets to enjoy Ladakh, or Badrinath, or Thachi valley — on schedule, and without the story turning into a cautionary tale. Sources: ' Ladakh Inner Line Permit: How to Apply, Fees & Areas 2026 ': Wanderon, Published 2026 ' Agumbe Ghat to remain closed till July 12 due to landslides ': Deccan Herald

items.title: From Kaziranga’s Floodwaters to Gold Theft: How K9 Leon Helped Crack Cases Across Assam
items.blurb: In the floodwaters of Kaziranga in 2019, a trail was almost invisible to the human eye. For K9 Leon, it wasn’t. The Belgian Malinois followed the scent of a suspect for nearly 20 km, moving across forest camps and security checkpoints. His tracking helped investigators identify and apprehend a suspected rhino poacher. Six years later, in a very different setting, his nose was put to work in a gold theft investigation in Golaghat. On 15 August 2026, Leon retired from active service during the Independence Day ceremony at Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve. Nearly eight years after joining the frontline, he leaves behind more than 200 patrols and over 30 specialised operations with Aaranyak’s K9 Sniffer Dog Squad, the Assam Forest Department, Kaziranga authorities and Assam Police. His handlers, Anil Kumar Das and Mrigen Das, worked alongside him throughout those years. 🐾Some heroes walk on two feet. Some leave pawprints behind. After nearly 8 years of service, K9 Leon retires during the Independence Day celebration at @kaziranga_ . With 200+ patrols and 30+ specialised operations, he helped protect Assam’s wildlife. Thank you, Leon. @NABU_de pic.twitter.com/M51hLNPZm0 — Aaranyak (@aaranyak) August 15, 2026 But Leon’s retirement also raises a fascinating question: what exactly is a wildlife sniffer dog smelling when it follows a poacher through a forest? And how can a dog’s nose find what people cannot? The trail humans miss A dog does not need to see a rhinoceros, a poacher or a piece of contraband to find it. It needs an odour. According to the IFAW-International Fund for Animal Welfare, wildlife detection dogs can be trained to identify scents associated with animal parts and derivatives, including those of rhinos, elephants and tigers . Depending on the assignment, dogs can also be trained to detect deer meat, live birds, snakes, porcupines, turtles and tortoises, as well as plant products such as red sanders. The principle is similar to that used to train dogs to detect drugs or explosives: a dog is introduced to a target scent and taught to indicate when it finds it. That makes dogs useful in places where conventional searches can be difficult — forests, vehicles, luggage, storage areas, shipping containers or even a trail that has long disappeared from human sight. The work begins with the nose. A nose built for clues Estimates vary by breed, but a dog’s sense of smell is thought to be between 100,000 and 100 million times more sensitive than that of humans. A much larger proportion of a dog’s brain is also dedicated to processing scent. The difference is not simply that dogs can smell more. They can separate smells. A dog can detect extremely low concentrations of an odour. Research cited by conservation detection experts compares this sensitivity to detecting the equivalent of a teaspoon of sugar in five million litres of water — roughly the volume of two Olympic-sized swimming pools. Dogs can also distinguish between closely related odours. Aaranyak’s dog unit was established as part of wider efforts to strengthen anti-poaching work in Assam, with support from NABU International. Photograph: (Aaranyak) Their nostrils give them another advantage. Each nostril can analyse the air independently, allowing a dog to detect small differences in scent concentration. Those differences can provide directional information: stronger on one side, weaker on the other, helping the dog adjust its path. Even the way dogs breathe works in their favour. The structure of their noses allows exhaled air to leave through the sides, reducing interference with incoming scents. This allows them to continue analysing odours while breathing in and out. For a tracker like Leon, this becomes a way of reading a landscape that humans cannot. But the nose has to learn A remarkable nose alone does not make a wildlife sniffer dog. Training teaches the dog what matters. Detection dogs are introduced to target scents and taught to associate finding them with a reward, often a toy or play. This is a form of classical, or Pavlovian, conditioning: the dog learns that identifying the correct scent leads to something it wants. Scent association can be one of the quicker parts of training. The harder work is teaching a dog to remain confident and safe in unfamiliar environments, particularly when the job involves forests, rivers, difficult terrain and long searches. For dogs that have come from troubled backgrounds, rehabilitation can take even longer. On 15 August 2026, Leon retired from active service during the Independence Day ceremony at Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve. Photograph: (Aaranyak) The relationship with the handler is equally important. A detection dog does not work alone. The dog searches, while the handler reads its behaviour, controls the operation and helps turn its indication into an investigation. Leon’s career shows the power of that partnership Leon completed a 12-month specialised training programme before joining active duty in November 2018. During the 2019 floods, he followed a scent trail for nearly 20 km that helped investigators trace a suspected rhino poacher. In 2023, after a deer carcass was discovered in the Bokakhat area, Leon’s tracking helped forest personnel locate crucial evidence and led them to four suspected poachers, according to Aaranyak. Then came a case far removed from Kaziranga’s forests. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Aaranyak (@aaranyak_india) In 2025, Leon assisted Assam Police in a gold theft investigation in Golaghat town. His scent-tracking work helped investigators identify and arrest four people allegedly involved in the theft. These cases show why conservation dogs can be useful for more than simply finding animals or chasing suspects. Their strongest contribution can be the evidence trail they help investigators recover. A different kind of conservation tool Wildlife crime rarely leaves a convenient trail. A poacher may move through dense vegetation, cross water, discard an object or leave an area before investigators arrive. Animal parts can also travel far beyond forests, making their way into vehicles, markets, warehouses and international trade routes. That is where scent detection adds another layer to enforcement. Aaranyak’s dog unit was established as part of wider efforts to strengthen anti-poaching work in Assam, with support from NABU International. Leon was among the dogs acquired in 2017, with specialised training preparing the unit for operational work. Leon’s retirement therefore marks more than the end of one working dog’s career. It also highlights how an ability dogs have always possessed — following a scent — can become a powerful conservation tool. On 15 August, Leon stopped going out on patrol. Aaranyak has said he will continue to receive proper care throughout his retirement. His working life took him through floodwaters, forest camps and riverine terrain, as well as investigations that stretched beyond wildlife crime. Now, after nearly eight years and hundreds of patrols, his routine will be quieter. But the trail he leaves behind is anything but. Sources: ‘New dogs join anti-poaching unit to protect rare rhino’ : By IFAW-International Fund for Animal Welfare, Published on 5 February 2026 ‘K9 dog squad tracking down poachers in Assam’ : By The Assam Tribune, Published on 19 August 2022
